description: Johnson Publishing Company (JPC), founded in Chicago in November 1942 by John H. Johnson, was the largest Black-owned publishing company of its era. name: John H. White
description: John H. White (born 1945 in Lexington, North Carolina) is an American photojournalist whose photographs of Black Chicago in 1973–74 are among the defining visual records of the city's South Side. Then a Chicago Daily News photographer, he was assigned by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency's DOCUMERICA program to photograph Chicago from June to October 1973 and again in the spring of 1974. His subject was the daily life of African American Chicago — activism, music, youth, housing, work, worship, and street life — rendered as a portrait of pride, love, and struggle. The work is held by the National Archives (series 412-DA), digitized and free of copyright restriction. White joined the Chicago Sun-Times in 1978 and remained on staff until May 2013; in 1982 he won the Pulitzer Prize for Photojournalism.

description: John Daniel Singleton (January 6, 1968 – April 2019) was an American director, screenwriter, and producer from South Central Los Angeles whose work represented the Black urban experience on screen. description: New Orleans/Louisiana bandleader who relocated to Chicago in 1919 and built the Creole Jazz Band, the bridge for the New Orleans-Chicago jazz migration.

name: John Lee Hooker
aliases: King of the Boogie; John Lee Booker (recording pseudonym)
description: Mississippi-born blues singer, guitarist, and songwriter (1917–2001) who developed the electric-guitar boogie in Detroit and recorded repeatedly in Chicago for the Black-owned Vee-Jay label: "Dimples" (1956) and "Boom Boom" (1962, R&B #16). Recorded 1951–52 for Chess and Chance Records as "John Lee Booker"; "Boogie Chillen'" (1948) was the best-selling race record of 1949. name: Joseph H. Jackson
aliases: Joseph Harrison Jackson; J. H. Jackson; Rev. J. H. Jackson
description: Pastor of Olivet Baptist Church, Chicago, 1941–1990; president of the National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc., 1953–1982 (29 years, the longest-serving presidency). Born September 11, 1900, near Rudyard, Mississippi; BA Jackson College 1926, BD Colgate Rochester 1932, MA Creighton 1934. The leading Black clerical voice against direct-action civil rights tactics — his 1964 address "The Vote is the Only Effective Weapon in the Civil Rights Struggle" crystallized the law-and-order alternative to Martin Luther King Jr. Installed L. Venchael Booth at First Baptist Church of Gary (1944); Booth later called the Progressive National Baptist Convention into being.

name: Jeff Donaldson
description: Chicago artist, art historian and AfriCOBRA founder; led the North American artists' delegation to FESTAC '77 in Lagos, Nigeria.

name: Jae Jarrell
description: Chicago AfriCOBRA artist; chaired the FESTAC '77 Committee of Creative Modern Black and African Dress and exhibited in Lagos.

name: Jacob H. Carruthers
aliases: Jacob H. Carruthers Jr.; Jacob Hudson Carruthers; Mzee Jedi Shemsu Jehewty
description: Chicago scholar and leading figure of the Kemetic/Afrocentric school; intellectual force behind the Kemetic Institute of Chicago.

name: Josef Ben Levi
description: Chicago-based retired scholar (Ed.D.) of ancient and continental philosophy, African American studies, education, sociology, curriculum, and disability studies. A student of Dr. Jacob H. Carruthers, he is a founding member and Associate Director of the Kemetic Institute of Chicago and a charter member of ASCAC; he teaches at the Jacob H. Carruthers Center for Inner City Studies (Northeastern Illinois University). Participant in the 1977 and 1978 CCICS Nile Valley study tours; chronicler of the Kemetic Institute's founding. Reads Ancient Egyptian, Arabic, Aramaic, Coptic, Hebrew, Meroitic, and Spanish.

name: Joel Augustus Rogers
aliases: Joel A. Rogers; J. A. Rogers
description: Jamaican-American journalist, historian and Chicago Art Institute student; covered Ethiopia's war with Italy and wrote for the Chicago Defender.

name: Jump Up Records
description: Chicago independent record label and mail-order distributor founded in 1993 by DJ Chuck Wren, specializing in original Jamaican ska, reggae, rocksteady, and calypso (200+ releases; vinyl-only ethos). Wren has hosted the ska radio show "Everything Off-Beat" since 1989 and runs Chicago's longest-running ska/reggae night at Delilah's.

name: Jerk, Seafood & Vegan Fest
description: The Jerk, Seafood & Vegan Fest — Martin's International's Chicago food festival celebrating Jamaican jerk, seafood, and vegan cuisines — launched in 2017 in connection with Martin's International's 35th anniversary; it honors Chicago founder Jean Baptiste Pointe DuSable and has combined editions with the African/Caribbean International Festival of Life.

name: Jazz Institute of Chicago
description: Nonprofit jazz presenting organization founded in 1969 by Art Hodes, Muhal Richard Abrams, Harriet Choice, Joe Segal, Bob Koester, Don DeMicheal, Jim DeJong, Penny Tyler (and John Steiner). Has programmed the Chicago Jazz Festival for the city since 1979; helped found the Chicago Jazz Archive at the University of Chicago.

name: Johnny Griffin
aliases: John Arnold Griffin III; Little Giant
description: Chicago-born hard-bop tenor saxophonist (1928–2008) known as the "Little Giant." Studied at DuSable High School under Walter Dyett; joined Lionel Hampton's band days after graduation (1945–47). Joined Art Blakey's Jazz Messengers (1957), recorded with Thelonious Monk (1958), succeeded John Coltrane in Monk's Five Spot quartet, and co-led a quintet with Eddie "Lockjaw" Davis (1960–62). Moved to France in 1963. Part of the Chicago tenor lineage alongside Von Freeman.

name: Jeffree
description: Singer Jeffree Perry, voice of the Chicago steppers anthems "Love's Gonna Last" and "Mr. Fix-It" (1979); brother of songwriter/producer Greg Perry and nephew of Robert Bateman; co-writer of Jackie Wilson's 'Beautiful Day'.

name: Jamila Woods
description: Jamila Woods is a South Side Chicago poet, singer, and multidisciplinary artist whose albums 'HEAVN', 'LEGACY! LEGACY!', and 'Water Made Us' work through Black feminist and Chicago themes.

name: J. W. Alexander
aliases: James Woodie Alexander II; James W. Alexander
description: Gospel singer, manager, songwriter, and producer (1916–1996); first tenor and manager of the Pilgrim Travelers; A&R man for Specialty Records who signed the Soul Stirrers (1950); Sam Cooke’s close associate and co-founder of SAR Records (1959), where he worked as a music publisher.

name: Jack Your Body — Steve 'Silk' Hurley
description: Steve 'Silk' Hurley's 'Jack Your Body' was released on DJ International Records in 1986 and reached No. 1 on the UK Singles Chart in January 1987 — the first house record to top the UK pop charts.

name: Jack Gibson ('Jack the Rapper')
aliases: Joseph Deighton Gibson Jr.; Jockey Jack; Jack the Rapper
description: Chicago-born Black radio pioneer ('Jockey Jack'); helped found WERD Atlanta (1949), the first Black-owned U.S. radio station; Motown's first national PR director; founder of the 'Mello Yello' trade paper and the annual Family Affairs convention.

name: Jesse B. Blayton Sr.
description: Atlanta accountant, banker, and broadcast pioneer: born December 6, 1897 in Fallis, Oklahoma; studied at the Walton School of Chicago and the University of Chicago before moving to Atlanta in 1922. Became Georgia's first Black Certified Public Accountant in 1928 (fourth African American nationwide); taught accounting at Atlanta University; was founding president of Mutual Federal Savings and Loan Association (1925-1971). In 1949 he bought 1,000-watt station WERD for $50,000, becoming the first African American to own and operate a radio station in the United States; WERD pioneered 'Negro appeal' programming for the local Black audience, and in the 1960s shared quarters with the SCLC. Sold WERD in 1968; died September 7, 1977; inducted into the Radio Hall of Fame in 1995.

name: John Simmons Negatives
description: The life's-work negatives of John Simmons (b. 1950, Chicago) — Chicago Defender photographer mentored by Bobby Sengstacke, later an Emmy-winning cinematographer — nearly lost in a garage fire and painstakingly salvaged; the 1965-1973 images anchor the 'No Crystal Stair' archive of Black Chicago street life.

name: Julieanna L. Richardson
description: Founder of The HistoryMakers (1999).

name: John Duke Kisch
description: American commercial photographer and archivist (born October 2, 1954, Miami, Florida); Bard College B.A. in photography (1976). Founder of the Separate Cinema Archive, begun in 1972 from a single gifted poster and grown over four decades to 37,000 objects documenting African American cinema from 1904 to the present - described as the most extensive private holding of African-American film memorabilia in the world. Author of 'A Separate Cinema: Fifty Years of Black-Cast Posters' (1992, foreword by Henry Louis Gates Jr., afterword by Spike Lee) and 'Separate Cinema: The First 100 Years of Black Poster Art' (2014). The Lucas Museum of Narrative Art acquired the archive. Lives in New York's Hudson Valley.

name: Johnson Publishing Company bankruptcy and archive auction
description: (2019-04 to 2019-07) Johnson Publishing Company filed for Chapter 7 bankruptcy protection on April 9, 2019. In July 2019 the company's Ebony/Jet photo archives - 4M+ images plus 10,000 hours of video and audio - were auctioned in Chicago; a four-foundation consortium (J. Paul Getty Trust as lead, Ford, MacArthur, Mellon) won with a $30M bid. The archives went to the Getty Research Institute and the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture. Context: JPC founded 1942 by John H. and Eunice Johnson; the magazines were sold in 2016; Mellody Hobson and George Lucas petitioned April 22, 2019 to take possession of the Ebony archive over a $12M collateralized loan; JPC's 87-piece art collection was auctioned in January 2020 (last major asset, just under $3M).

name: John Simmons garage fire
description: Fire (and water damage) that destroyed nearly all of Chicago photographer John Simmons's photographic negatives: while planning to move apartments, he stored his work in a friend's garage; days later the garage caught fire. Negatives were found stuck together and tainted by water damage; a painstaking salvage followed, with some images still unrecovered. Reported by Hyperallergic in April 2019 - the fire therefore predates April 2019; the exact date is unspecified in the source. Simmons is an Emmy Award-winning cinematographer and UCLA professor of cinematography.

name: John Hope Franklin estate sale
description: (2017-02) The February 2017 estate sale of the late historian John Hope Franklin's personal effects at his Durham, N.C. home - organized by Gay Gasper Pleasant's estate company after his 2009 death; thousands of books (hundreds on slavery, the South, the Civil War and Reconstruction) drew collectors, historians, and fans who lined up hours early. A CTL PRESERVE-001 warning case about eminent scholars' materials dispersing at tag sale: Franklin's scholarly papers went instead to Duke University's Rubenstein Library (300+ boxes donated by his family), and the John Hope Franklin Research Center had been established at Duke in 1995 on his own papers donation.

name: JPC archive transfer to NMAAHC/Getty
description: Transfer of the Johnson Publishing Company photo archive to joint Smithsonian National Museum of African American History and Culture / Getty Research Institute ownership, announced 2022-07-28 (consortium: Ford Foundation, J. Paul Getty Trust, MacArthur Foundation, Mellon Foundation, Smithsonian Institution). Getty committed $30M to processing and digitization toward public availability. Followed JPC's April 2019 Chapter 7 filing and the July 2019 $30M auction. Advisory council (chaired by Librarian of Congress Carla Hayden) formed 2020. NMAAHC director Kevin Young: the archive gave African Americans 'an authentic public representation of themselves.' Portions accessible during ongoing digitization. (A September 6, 2022 report describes the formal transfer; see conflict CTL-CFL-002184.)

name: J.M. Higginbotham
description: J.M. Higginbotham: African American architect practicing in early-20th-century Chicago, described as one of America's first African American architects; designed the Olivet Building. Liberty Baptist Church purchased the Olivet Building in 1924; under Rev. D.Z. Jackson (minister from 1925) membership grew from the hundreds to 3,000+. Congregation moved to 56 E. 46th St, then built at 49th and South Park Way (plans 1950, groundbreaking 1952). In 1966 Martin Luther King Jr. chose Liberty Baptist as his Chicago headquarters.

name: Jackson Park branch (now East 63rd branch, CTA Green Line)
aliases: East 63rd branch; Jackson Park elevated branch
description: CTA elevated branch built directly over 63rd Street for the 1893 World's Columbian Exposition. Truncated over the 20th century; the structure east of Cottage Grove was demolished September 27, 1997. Now the East 63rd branch of the Green Line.

name: Jackson Park (Stony Island) CTA station site
aliases: Stony Island station; Jackson Park station
description: Former CTA Green Line (Jackson Park branch) station at Stony Island Avenue and 63rd Street, Woodlawn. Opened May 12, 1893 as 'Stony Island' for the World's Columbian Exposition; service suspended March 4, 1982 (bridge defect over the Illinois Central), never restored east of University; the branch east of Cottage Grove was demolished September 27, 1997.

name: Jack Wiener
aliases: Jack Weiner; Jack Sheldon Wiener; Sheldon Wiener
description: Chicago audio engineer Jack Sheldon Wiener; built and ran Sheldon Recording Studios and was the one-third partner who designed the 2120 S. Michigan studio for Leonard and Phil Chess. His name is commonly misspelled "Jack Weiner".

name: Jalaiah Harmon
description: Fayetteville, Georgia dancer and content creator who choreographed the viral Renegade dance (September 2019); her fight for credit became a landmark case on creator attribution in the platform era.

description: Surinamese-American inventor whose automated lasting machine (U.S. Patent 274,207, March 20, 1883) mechanized shoe lasting, multiplying output and roughly halving shoe prices.

name: Jesse Eugene Russell
description: African American electrical engineer and inventor (born April 26, 1948, Nolensville, Tennessee): B.S. in electrical engineering from Tennessee State University (1972) - the first African American hired directly from an HBCU by AT&T Bell Laboratories - and M.S. from Stanford University (1973). At Bell Labs he pioneered digital cellular communications; in 1988 he led the first Bell Labs team to introduce digital cellular technology in the United States. Holds 100+ wireless patents, including U.S. Patent 5,084,869 (1992) for digital cellular base station design. Later chairman and CEO of incNETWORKS, Inc.; inducted into the National Academy of Engineering.

name: John Pasmore
description: Computer scientist and entrepreneur; founder and CEO of the AI startup Latimer and CEO of FutureSum AI. Created the Latimer large language model - named after 19th-century Black inventor Lewis Latimer - as a technological answer to racial bias in popular LLMs, using a retrieval-augmented generation approach over data sources including books and newspapers by Black writers, in partnership with HBCUs. Earlier: partnered with Russell Simmons (1995-2005) to create Oneworld Media (CEO); co-founder and CEO of the video travel platform VoyageTV; partner at TRS Capital.

name: Joy Buolamwini
description: Computer scientist and 'poet of code' (Rhodes Scholar): B.S. in computer science from Georgia Tech (Stamps President's Scholar); master's degrees from Oxford (Learning and Technology) and MIT. As a researcher at the MIT Media Lab, her 2018 thesis project 'Gender Shades' uncovered large racial and gender bias in commercial AI gender classification (Microsoft, IBM, Amazon systems), prompting IBM and Microsoft to take corrective action. Coined 'The Coded Gaze.' Founder of the Algorithmic Justice League (still its director), leading a movement for equitable, accountable AI. TED Talk 'How I'm fighting bias in algorithms' (~1.5M views); author of 'Unmasking AI: My Mission to Protect What Is Human in a World of Machines' (2023).

name: Joseph H. Jefferson
description: Co-founder (with Balm L. Leavell) of the Chicago Crusader in 1940; held the majority interest and served as co-publisher. The Crusader was published in the Ida B. Wells Housing Development, financed with donations, and became Chicago's longest-running African-American weekly ("The Militant Voice of the People"). With Leavell he extended the group to Gary with the Gary Crusader. After Leavell's 1968 death he supported Dorothy Leavell's succession as publisher.

name: Jackie Ormes
description: Cartoonist Zelda Mavin Jackson, widely considered the first African-American woman cartoonist; creator of Torchy Brown, Patty-Jo 'n' Ginger, and Candy for the Pittsburgh Courier and the Chicago Defender.

name: Joseph Dandridge Bibb
description: African American journalist and editor (1882–1945). Associate editor (co-editor) of the Chicago Whip; after founder William C. Linton's death in March 1922, Bibb took over the paper. Under his editorship the Whip's "Don't Spend Money Where You Can't Work" campaign boycotted discriminatory white-run businesses and helped more than 15,000 Chicago Blacks secure jobs; the paper reached 65,000 circulation within a year of its 1919 launch and published until 1939 as the Chicago Defender's chief contemporary rival.

description: Founder and editor of The Broad Ax (1895), the Black weekly he launched in Salt Lake City, Utah, and moved to Chicago in 1899. Born in Virginia in 1854 to an enslaved couple (Zinn Education Project; the inherited stub era field records 1847 — see CTL-CFL-002243). A Democratic partisan and atheist in Mormon-dominated Utah, he was appointed one of the first Black jurors west of the Mississippi; his paper was called the most controversial Black newspaper in late-19th-century Chicago, noted for criticizing Booker T. Washington.

name: JPC Photo Archive (NMAAHC + Getty)
description: Ebony/Jet photographic archive of the Johnson Publishing Company: 3.35M negatives and slides, 983,000 photographs, 166,000 contact sheets, 9,000 audio/visual recordings - the most significant collection illustrating African American life in the 20th century (WWII through the civil rights movement and the 1980s-90s culture boom). JPC founded 1942 by John H. and Eunice W. Johnson (Ebony 1945, Jet 1951); magazines sold 2016, archive retained; JPC Chapter 7 (2019-04) led to the July 2019 auction. Acquired for $30M by the Ford, J. Paul Getty Trust, MacArthur, Mellon, and Smithsonian consortium; ownership transferred to joint NMAAHC/Getty Research Institute stewardship (announced 2022-07-28); Getty committed $30M to processing and digitization; archive housed at NMAAHC, Washington D.C., with the Chicago-pertinent portion to remain permanently in Chicago.

name: Joseph Harrison Jackson
description: Baptist minister (September 11, 1900 - August 18, 1990), born near Rudyard, Mississippi; B.A. Jackson College (1926), B.D. Colgate Rochester Divinity School (1932), M.A. Creighton University (1934); ordained at 22, pastor of First Baptist Church, McComb, Mississippi. Moved to Chicago in 1941 to pastor Olivet Baptist Church, serving until his death in 1990; membership grew from ~10,000 to over 20,000. Elected president of the National Baptist Convention, USA, Inc. in Miami in September 1953 and headed it for 29 years (to 1982). Often clashed with Martin Luther King Jr., opposing the use of civil disobedience in the civil rights movement. Charter member of the World Council of Churches (1937, 1948 planning conferences); vice president of the Baptist World Alliance.

name: Johnny P
description: Chicago R&B singer (born Johnny Pigram; d. 2016), the go-to hook singer of mid-1990s Chicago rap. Sang the hook on Do or Die's "Po Pimp" (1996, feat. Twista — #22 Hot 100, #1 Hot Rap Singles, gold), the follow-up "Playa Like Me and You," and Scarface's "Smile" (1997, feat. 2Pac). Released the teen R&B debut "Connect the Dots" (1989, Columbia) and "The Next" (1998, Rap-A-Lot). Died November 27, 2016, at 44.

name: Jackie Robinson West Little League
description: Black-governed youth baseball league on the South Side: structured recreation, leadership and discipline formation, and community cohesion Geography: Chicago, Illinois (South Side)

name: Jack L. Cooper and The All-Negro Hour
description: Jack L. Cooper and The All-Negro Hour names the landmark Chicago radio program created, produced, and hosted by Jack L. Cooper. The All-Negro Hour debuted on Chicago's WSBC on November 3, 1929, a Sunday-night variety hour of gospel, jazz, blues, sermons, and comedy — the first radio program in U.S. history to feature Black performers exclusively, and the broadcast that made Cooper the first African American radio announcer and the first Black disc jockey. By the mid-1930s Cooper was producing about nine hours of programming a week; in 1947 his production company controlled forty hours a week across four Chicago stations. He retired in 1959 and was inducted into the National Radio Hall of Fame in 2012. Almost none of the original broadcasts survive, because WSBC did not preserve its transcription discs.

name: Jumping the broom
description: Wedding ritual in which the couple leaps over a broom to seal the union. Originated among enslaved Black people denied legal marriage as a public declaration of union before witnesses; fell out of use after emancipation and was revived in the late 20th century after Alex Haley's Roots (1976 novel; 1977 ABC miniseries) depicted Kunta Kinte jumping the broom with Bell. Origins are disputed: the African American Registry traces Asante/Akan Ghanaian roots, while researcher Imani G. Strong holds the adoption mechanism unknowable (see CTL-CFL-002245).

name: Johnson Products Company (Afro Sheen / Ultra Sheen)
description: Johnson Products Company — founded 1954 on Chicago's South Side by George and Joan Johnson with a $250 loan — became the first Black-owned company listed on the American Stock Exchange (1971), creator of Afro Sheen and Ultra Sheen, exclusive sponsor of Soul Train; sold to Ivax in 1993, returned to Black ownership in March 2009.

name: Jiffy Cab — Black-owned jitney cabs on the South Side
description: Black-owned jitney cab service remembered on Chicago's South Side (King Drive area), filling gaps left by mainstream cab companies that would not serve Black neighborhoods.

name: John W. Moutoussamy
description: Chicago architect (1922–1995), the first African American partner in a large Chicago architectural firm (Dubin, Dubin, Black & Moutoussamy). Studied at the Illinois Institute of Technology under Mies van der Rohe (class of 1948). Designed the Johnson Publishing Company headquarters at 820 S. Michigan Avenue (built 1969–71, dedicated May 16, 1972) — the only downtown Chicago high-rise designed by an African American (Chicago Landmark, 2017). Also designed Daley College, Olive–Harvey College, Truman College, the Chicago Urban League building, and the Regents Park Twin Towers in Hyde Park.

name: Jones brothers enterprises
description: The Jones brothers' enterprises — the policy (numbers) empire run by Edward 'Big Ed' Jones with his brothers George and Mack in 1930s-40s Bronzeville — the dominant Black-run gambling economy of the Black Belt, which reinvested profits in the community and became the ancestor of the Illinois Lottery.

name: Jordan Building
description: A three-story combination store and apartment building commissioned by Black songwriter and music publisher Joseph J. Jordan; the 1985 NPS Black Metropolis nomination identifies it as the start of the series of Black-owned/financed building projects on South State in the 1920s.

name: James P. Johnson
description: James P. Johnson was a pianist associated with the development of stride piano — the Google Arts & Culture claim carried in his record — and is named in CultureTechLens's rent-party research as the father of stride and the rent party's house musician. Harlem's rent parties were stride's laboratory: Johnson played them constantly, introduced the teenage Fats Waller to the scene and brought him to parties where they performed, and the head-to-head cutting contests held in apartment parlors shaped the style itself — its thunderous left hand, breakneck tempos, and showmanship. The standard biography is Scott E. Brown's James P. Johnson: A Case of Mistaken Identity (Scarecrow Press, 1986), with Brown's Speakeasies to Symphonies (University Press of Mississippi, 2026) as its in-print companion. He is cataloged CTL-JAZZ-011 in the CTL-JAZZ-100 dataset.

name: James Brown
description: James Brown (born May 3, 1933, in Barnwell, South Carolina; died December 25, 2006, in Atlanta, Georgia) was an American singer, bandleader, and producer who built funk out of soul and gospel. Raised in Augusta, Georgia, he rose as lead singer of the Famous Flames and broke through with “Please, Please, Please” (1956). Live at the Apollo (1963) captured his incendiary stage act and stayed on the charts for 66 weeks. Singles such as “Papa's Got a Brand New Bag,” “I Got You (I Feel Good),” and “Say It Loud — I'm Black and I'm Proud” (1968) made rhythm itself the message. He played Chicago's Regal Theater repeatedly in the 1960s, including a documented engagement in May 1967. History's honorific for him — the Godfather of Soul — records the debt later music owes. In 1986 he was among the first artists inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame.

name: Jack Delano
description: Jack Delano (1914–1997) was a Ukrainian-born American photographer and composer. Born Jacob Ovcharov in Voroshilovka, near Kyiv, he immigrated to the United States with his family in 1923 and graduated from the Pennsylvania Academy of the Fine Arts in 1937. He joined the Farm Security Administration as a photographer in 1940 and continued under its successor agency, the Office of War Information. In the winter of 1942–43, on a six-month assignment to document the wartime railroad industry, Delano worked mostly in Chicago — the nation's railroad hub — producing some 3,000 photographs, nearly 2,000 of them in and around the city: yard and shop crews, railroaders' portraits, and his celebrated color view inside Chicago Union Station. A 1941 FSA trip to Puerto Rico changed the course of his life; he settled there permanently in 1946 and built a second career as a composer drawing on Puerto Rican folk material.

name: Juice WRLD
description: Jarad Anthony Higgins, known as Juice WRLD, was a rapper, singer and songwriter from the Chicago area who became the defining voice of emo rap's mainstream breakthrough before his death at twenty-one. Raised in Calumet Park and Homewood, he played piano, drums and guitar as a child, began freestyling in high school, and first recorded as JuiceTheKidd, taking his later name from the film Juice. His 2018 singles "All Girls Are the Same" and "Lucid Dreams" — the latter built on a Sting interpolation and eventually certified diamond — carried his debut album Goodbye & Good Riddance onto the charts, and his second album, Death Race for Love (2019), debuted at number one. His writing confronted heartbreak, anxiety and addiction with unusual directness, and posthumous releases including Legends Never Die have kept his catalog at the center of his generation's listening. He died on December 8, 2019, days after his twenty-first birthday; the Cook County Medical Examiner later ruled the death an accidental overdose. He is remembered with love by the fans — the 999 faithful — for whom his honesty was a lifeline.

name: Jhené Aiko
description: Los Angeles singer and songwriter whose light, expressive soprano and unhurried, confessional writing helped define the sound of alternative R&B in the 2010s. Born Jhené Aiko Efuru Chilombo on March 16, 1988, in Los Angeles, she first sang as a teenager contributing backing vocals for the R&B group B2K, then stepped away to finish her education before returning with the self-written mixtape Sailing Soul(s) in 2011. Her breakthrough came in 2013, when her feature on Big Sean's single Beware became her first Top 40 hit and she released the EP Sail Out, whose single The Worst reached No. 43 on the Billboard Hot 100. Her debut studio album Souled Out followed in 2014, the collaborative project Twenty88 with Big Sean in 2016, and the expansive Trip in 2017. Her third album, Chilombo (2020), which folds crystal singing-bowl tones into her arrangements, earned three Grammy nominations including Album of the Year and stands as the fullest statement of her healing-centered artistry.

name: James Meredith
aliases: James Howard Meredith; James H. Meredith
description: James Meredith, born James Howard Meredith in Kosciusko, Mississippi, in 1933, is an American civil rights figure, writer and Air Force veteran whose decision to attend his state's flagship university became a national test of federal law. After service in the United States Air Force from 1951 to 1960 and study at Jackson State College, he applied to the segregated University of Mississippi. Rejected because of his race, he sued with NAACP support, and federal courts ordered his admission. Governor Ross Barnett blocked him physically, rioting followed when he reached the Oxford campus under federal protection on September 30, 1962, and two people were killed. Meredith began classes on October 1, 1962, as the university's first Black student, and graduated in political science in 1963. He later earned a law degree from Columbia University. In June 1966 he began a solitary March Against Fear from Memphis to Jackson to encourage Black voter registration; a sniper wounded him on the second day, other leaders continued the march, and Meredith recovered, rejoined it, and entered Jackson with thousands of marchers on June 26.

name: John Brown's Raid on Harpers Ferry (1859)
aliases: John Brown's Raid; Harpers Ferry Raid
description: On the night of October 16, 1859, the abolitionist John Brown led twenty-one men — including five Black men: Dangerfield Newby, Lewis Leary, John Copeland Jr., Shields Green, and Osborne Perry Anderson — in a raid on the federal armory at Harpers Ferry, Virginia (now West Virginia). Brown intended to seize weapons and establish a stronghold from which enslaved people could be armed and freed, beginning a liberation campaign through the Appalachian South. The raiders held the armory briefly before being cornered in its fire-engine house by local militia and a detachment of United States Marines under Colonel Robert E. Lee; ten raiders were killed, and Brown was captured, tried for treason against Virginia, and hanged at Charles Town on December 2, 1859. The raid electrified the country — condemned across the South as proof of Northern intent, mourned in the North with church bells and eulogies — and it stands, eighteen months before Fort Sumter, as the violent overture to the Civil War. The graph already holds Brown the man (CTL-E-1586); this record holds the act.

name: Jackie Robinson
description: Jack Roosevelt Robinson (born January 31, 1919, in Cairo, Georgia) broke modern Major League Baseball's color line on April 15, 1947, when he took the field at first base for the Brooklyn Dodgers at Ebbets Field — the event the intake timeline files simply under his name and year. Signed by Branch Rickey and seasoned with the Kansas City Monarchs of the Negro American League and the Dodgers' Montreal farm club, Robinson endured the abuse Rickey had warned him to absorb without retaliation, and answered with his play: National League Rookie of the Year in 1947, Most Valuable Player in 1949, a World Series championship in 1955, and election to the Baseball Hall of Fame in 1962, the first year he was eligible. After baseball he wrote, broadcast, marched, and raised money for the movement, carrying the integration fight far beyond the diamond. He died in 1972, aged fifty-three. In 1997 Major League Baseball retired his number 42 across the entire sport. The graph held a Chicago Little League bearing his name (CTL-E-1253) before it held the man; this record corrects that order.

name: Jesse Jackson Presidential Campaign (1984)
aliases: Jesse Jackson 1984 Campaign; Rainbow Coalition Campaign of 1984
description: In the 1984 election cycle, the Reverend Jesse Jackson Sr. — the Chicago organizer held at CTL-E-0083 — ran for the Democratic presidential nomination, announcing his candidacy on November 3, 1983, and building the campaign he called the Rainbow Coalition: Black voters, organized in numbers no campaign had previously sought, joined with farmers, union members, Latinos, Asian Americans, and the white working poor in a single insurgent coalition. Jackson won roughly 3.3 million primary votes — about eighteen percent of the total — carried five primary and caucus contests, and finished third for the nomination behind Walter Mondale and Gary Hart. His campaign registered an estimated two million new voters, demonstrated that a Black candidate could assemble a national primary electorate, and forced the Democratic Party to renegotiate its delegate rules at the 1984 convention, where Jackson addressed the hall in one of the era's defining convention speeches. He ran again, larger, in 1988. The intake timeline's language — 'Jesse Jackson Galvanizes Black Voters' — is the correct verb: the measurable legacy of 1984 is registration rolls that stayed changed.

name: Jack Johnson
description: John Arthur “Jack” Johnson (March 31, 1878 – June 10, 1946), the “Galveston Giant,” was the first Black world heavyweight boxing champion, holding the title from 1908 to 1915 in the heart of the Jim Crow era. Born in Galveston, Texas, he won the World Colored Heavyweight title in 1903 and, after white champions refused him a title shot for years, defeated Tommy Burns in Sydney on December 26, 1908. His July 4, 1910 victory over former champion James J. Jeffries — the “Fight of the Century” — triggered race riots across the United States. Chicago became his adopted stage: on July 10, 1912, he opened the Café de Champion, an opulent desegregated “black and tan” club at 41 West 31st Street in Bronzeville, and lived above it. Convicted under the Mann Act in a prosecution widely regarded as racially motivated, he fled abroad in 1913, surrendered in 1920, and served his sentence at Leavenworth. He died in a North Carolina car crash in 1946, was buried at Chicago's Graceland Cemetery, entered the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1990, and received a posthumous presidential pardon in 2018.

name: J. Cole
description: J. Cole (born Jermaine Lamarr Cole, January 28, 1985, at a U.S. military base in Frankfurt, West Germany) is an American rapper and producer raised in Fayetteville, North Carolina. After his debut mixtape The Come Up (2007), he signed with Jay-Z's Roc Nation in 2009, releasing The Warm Up (2009) and Friday Night Lights (2010). Every one of his studio albums has topped the Billboard 200, from Cole World: The Sideline Story (2011) through Born Sinner (2013), 2014 Forest Hills Drive (2014), KOD (2018), and The Off-Season (2021). He founded Dreamville Records and built the Dreamville Festival in Fayetteville. The Fall-Off (2026) — the subject of CTL Short #49 — was marketed as his final album: a double album built on two returns to Fayetteville, at twenty-nine and at thirty-nine, debuting at No. 1.

name: Jeff Parker
description: Jeff Parker (born April 4, 1967, in Bridgeport, Connecticut) is an American guitarist and composer. Raised in Hampton, Virginia, and trained at Berklee College of Music, he moved to Chicago in 1991 and joined the Association for the Advancement of Creative Musicians (CTL-E-0290) in 1995, embedding himself in the city's creative-music underground — co-founding Isotope 217 and the Chicago Underground ensembles with Rob Mazurek, and joining the post-rock group Tortoise in time for its album TNT (1998). His solo records, including The Relatives (2005), The New Breed (2016), Suite for Max Brown (2020), and Forfolks (2021), blend post-bop, funk, and hip-hop production. Since 2016 his ETA IVtet — Anna Butterss, Jay Bellerose, and Josh Johnson — formed around a Monday residency at Los Angeles's Enfield Tennis Academy bar, has released Mondays at the Enfield Tennis Academy (2022), The Way Out of Easy (2024), and Happy Today (2026), the subject of CTL Short #52.

name: Jabari Parker
description: Jabari Parker (born March 15, 1995, in Chicago, Illinois) is an American professional basketball player whose career begins at Simeon Career Academy in Chicago. At Simeon he plays alongside Kendrick Nunn (CTL-E-5588) and leads the Wolverines to four consecutive Illinois Class 4A state championships, winning Illinois Mr. Basketball twice and the Gatorade National Player of the Year award in 2012. After one season at Duke — consensus first-team All-American, national freshman of the year, and ACC Rookie of the Year in 2014 — Milwaukee selects him second overall in the 2014 NBA draft. Two tears of the anterior cruciate ligament in his left knee interrupt his time with the Bucks. He signs with his hometown Chicago Bulls in 2018, later plays for Washington, Atlanta, Sacramento, and Boston in the NBA, and continues his career in Europe with FC Barcelona from 2023 and Partizan Belgrade from 2025.

name: Jahlil Okafor
description: Jahlil Obika Okafor (born December 15, 1995, in Fort Smith, Arkansas) is a Nigerian-American professional basketball player formed in Chicago. After his mother dies when he is nine, he moves in with his father on Chicago's South Side, and the family later moves to the North Side so he can attend Whitney M. Young Magnet High School, where he becomes the nation's top recruit and wins Illinois Mr. Basketball and national player of the year honors in 2014. In one season at Duke he averages 17.3 points and 8.5 rebounds, becomes the first freshman named ACC Player of the Year, and helps the Blue Devils win the 2015 NCAA championship. Philadelphia selects him third overall in the 2015 NBA draft, and he averages 17.5 points as a rookie on the NBA All-Rookie First Team. His later career runs through Brooklyn, New Orleans, Detroit, and Indiana, and through clubs overseas, reaching Levanga Hokkaido in Japan in 2025.

name: Jeremih
description: Jeremih, born Jeremy Phillip Felton on July 17, 1987, in Chicago, Illinois, is an American R&B singer, songwriter, and producer from Chicago's South Side. He plays drums from age three, learns other instruments, and briefly studies engineering before entering the music business program at Columbia College Chicago. There he partners with producer Mick Schultz, and their work attracts a recording contract with Def Jam Recordings in 2009. His debut single, “Birthday Sex,” peaks at number four on the Billboard Hot 100, and his self-titled debut album reaches number six on the Billboard 200 that year. He follows with All About You in 2010, featuring “Down on Me” with 50 Cent, and Late Nights: The Album in 2015, preceded by the 2014 top-ten single “Don't Tell 'Em” featuring YG. In 2018 he forms the duo MihTy with Ty Dolla $ign. In November 2020 he is hospitalized in Chicago with COVID-19, placed on a ventilator in intensive care, and is released from hospital in December.

name: Jackie Aina
description: Jackie Aina (born August 4, 1987, in Los Angeles) is a Nigerian-American beauty creator who built one of YouTube's most influential makeup channels by reviewing products for deep skin tones and publicly challenging the beauty industry on shade range. She launched her channel in 2009 while serving in the United States Army Reserve, and her advocacy became structural in 2018, when Too Faced expanded its Born This Way foundation from 24 to 35 shades in collaboration with her — nine of the eleven new shades formulated by Aina. That year she won the NAACP Image Award for YouTuber of the Year, the category's inaugural year. TIME named her one of the 25 most influential people on the internet in 2019. In July 2020 she co-founded the home fragrance and lifestyle brand FORVR Mood with Denis Asamoah. CultureTechLens profiled Aina in Short #97, published October 13, 2026.

name: Jeanette Taylor
aliases: Jeanette Beatrice Taylor; Ald. Jeanette Taylor
description: Jeanette Taylor, born Jeanette Beatrice Taylor on May 15, 1975, in Chicago, Illinois, is the alderwoman of Chicago's 20th Ward, covering Woodlawn and parts of the South Side. The daughter of a Chicago Public Schools clerk and a taxi driver, she graduated from Dunbar Vocational High School and was elected at 19 to the local school council of Mollison Elementary School, where she served for more than twenty years. As an organizer with the Kenwood Oakland Community Organization, she helped lead the 2015 hunger strike — 34 days, twelve strikers — that forced the city to keep Walter H. Dyett High School open. In 2019 she won the open 20th Ward seat vacated by Willie Cochran and took office on May 20, 2019, as a member of the City Council's Democratic Socialist caucus. Her signature fight has been anti-displacement: she co-introduced the community benefits ordinance for the Obama Presidential Center and negotiated the 2020 compromise that added affordable-housing protections around it. She was re-elected in February 2023, clearing 50 percent in the first round.

name: James Reynolds Jr
description: James Reynolds Jr. is a Chicago financier, the founder, chairman, and chief executive officer of Loop Capital, the investment bank he established in 1997 with Albert R. Grace Jr. Reynolds built his early career in municipal finance in Chicago, establishing and leading the Midwest Municipal Bond Sales Desk at PaineWebber and then managing municipal sales for the Midwest at Merrill Lynch's Corporate and Institutional Client Group. Loop Capital began as a municipal bond firm and grew under his leadership into one of the largest privately held investment banks in the United States and the nation's largest minority-owned financial services firm, spanning investment banking, brokerage, public finance, and asset management; in 2015 Loop partnered with Magic Johnson Enterprises to form JLC Infrastructure. Reynolds chairs the board of the Chicago Community Trust, has chaired the Securities Industry and Financial Markets Association, and serves on boards including World Business Chicago and the Chicago Urban League. He was inducted into the Bond Buyer Hall of Fame.

name: Jean Grae
description: Jean Grae (born Tsidi Ibrahim on November 26, 1976, in Cape Town, South Africa) is the underground's lyricist's lyricist — born to South African jazz royalty, pianist Abdullah Ibrahim and vocalist Sathima Bea Benjamin, and raised in Manhattan's Hotel Chelsea. She studied vocal performance at LaGuardia High School, came up in the group Natural Resource under the name What? What?, and took her solo name from the X-Men's Jean Grey. Her debut Attack of the Attacking Things (2002) and This Week (2004) built a cult on polysyllabic, dry-witted writing; Jeanius (2008), produced by 9th Wonder, drew Robert Christgau's praise on NPR for its "rapidity, clarity and idiomatic cadence." In 2018 she released Everything's Fine with Quelle Chris, her partner, a satire of American anxiety that extended her second career as a writer and humorist. name: Jeff Friday
description: Jeff Friday is an American entertainment executive from Newark, New Jersey, who founded the American Black Film Festival (CTL-E-5637). An advertising executive — he left the presidency of the multicultural agency UniWorld Group to build the festival — he attended the Sundance Film Festival in January 1997, saw how few Black filmmakers, executives and stories were in the room, and four months later launched the first edition in Acapulco, Mexico, with his former boss and investor Byron E. Lewis and filmmaker Warrington Hudlin, drawing about 600 people. Friday later acquired full rights to the festival, renamed it the American Black Film Festival, and moved it to Miami, building it with his wife, co-founder Nicole Friday, into the leading U.S. festival platform for Black film — through ABFF Ventures (now operating as Nice Crowd, where he is founder and CEO) and Jeff Friday Media, the production company he formed in 2019. The festival's record in this graph has carried its founded_by edge as blocked since Shorts Wave 4; this record is the founder.

name: James Baldwin
aliases: James Arthur Jones; James Arthur Baldwin
description: James Baldwin (born James Arthur Jones on August 2, 1924, in Harlem, New York) was the novelist and essayist who became the moral witness of the American civil rights era. A teenage preacher in Harlem, he left for Paris in 1948 and published Go Tell It on the Mountain (1953), Notes of a Native Son (1955) and Giovanni's Room (1956). The Fire Next Time (1963) — two letters on race, faith and the American future — made him a national figure, and his essays, novels and speeches carried the movement's case in a prose no contemporary matched. He died of stomach cancer at his home in Saint-Paul-de-Vence, France, in late 1987 — reference works differ by a day on the date, giving November 30 and December 1; this record follows November 30 and prints the variance. He had been made a Commander of the French Legion of Honour in 1986. His unfinished manuscript Remember This House became the 2016 documentary I Am Not Your Negro. description: Jacquees, born Rodriquez Jacquees Broadnax on 15 April in Decatur, Georgia, is an American R&B singer. A Decatur native who sang in talent shows from childhood, he signed to Birdman's Cash Money Records in 2014 and released the EP 19 that year. His breakthrough single "B.E.D." (2016) reached No. 69 on the Hot 100 and was certified 2× platinum; the debut studio album 4275 followed in 2018 on Cash Money and Republic. His second album took its title from his self-proclaimed crown, King of R&B (2019) — a claim that drew public debate — and peaked at No. 20 on the Billboard 200; Sincerely For You followed in 2022, and he is a member of Rich Gang. name: Joey Meyer
description: Joey Meyer (born April 2, 1949, in Chicago; died December 29, 2023, in Hinsdale, Illinois) was an American basketball player and coach whose career was spent almost entirely at DePaul University. He played guard for the Blue Demons from 1968 to 1971 under his father, head coach Ray Meyer, finishing with 1,233 career points, then served eleven seasons as his father's assistant before succeeding him as head coach in 1984. In thirteen seasons as DePaul's head coach, 1984 to 1997, Meyer compiled a 231–158 record, the second-most wins in program history behind his father, and led the Blue Demons to seven NCAA tournament appearances, including back-to-back Sweet Sixteen runs in 1986 and 1987. He was named Chevrolet National Coach of the Year in 1987 and led DePaul to its first conference title, the 1992 Great Midwest Conference regular-season championship. After DePaul he coached in the NBA's developmental league and worked as a regional scout for the Los Angeles Clippers. DePaul announced his death on December 29, 2023, at the age of 74.

name: Junior M.A.F.I.A.
aliases: Junior Masters At Finding Intelligent Attitudes
description: Junior M.A.F.I.A. was an American hip-hop group from Brooklyn, New York, assembled and mentored by The Notorious B.I.G., who acted as the group's godfather; its name is an acronym for Junior Masters At Finding Intelligent Attitudes. Its members included Lil' Kim, Lil' Cease, Trife, Larceny, Nino Brown, Chico Del Vec and MC Klepto. The group released its debut album, Conspiracy, on August 29, 1995, through Big Beat Records and B.I.G.'s Undeas imprint; it debuted at number eight on the Billboard 200 and was later certified gold by the RIAA. B.I.G. appeared on four of the album's tracks. The lead single, 'Player's Anthem,' featuring B.I.G., was certified gold, and 'Get Money,' a duet between B.I.G. and Lil' Kim, was certified platinum and helped launch Kim's solo career ahead of her debut album Hard Core (1996). The group effectively ended after B.I.G. was killed in 1997. Both endpoints of its defining relationship hold records in this graph — The Notorious B.I.G. (CTL-E-5702) and Lil' Kim (CTL-E-5668) — and this record completes the member wiring both of their packets documented as blocked.

name: Jimi Hendrix
aliases: James Marshall Hendrix; Johnny Allen Hendrix
description: Jimi Hendrix, born Johnny Allen Hendrix on 27 November 1942 in Seattle, Washington, was an American guitarist, singer and composer who redefined the electric guitar. He took up the guitar at fifteen, served briefly in the U.S. Army in 1961–62, and then worked the Chitlin' Circuit, backing the Isley Brothers and, through mid-1965, Little Richard. Moving to London in late 1966 under manager Chas Chandler, he formed the Jimi Hendrix Experience with bassist Noel Redding and drummer Mitch Mitchell and scored three UK Top 10 hits: "Hey Joe," "Purple Haze" and "The Wind Cries Mary." His 1967 Monterey Pop Festival performance made him famous in the United States. His third album, Electric Ladyland (1968), was his only No. 1 album on the Billboard 200. He headlined Woodstock in 1969 and the Isle of Wight Festival in 1970. Hendrix died in London on 18 September 1970, at age 27, after a recording career as a featured artist of only four years. The Jimi Hendrix Experience were inducted into the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 1992.

name: Jaafar Jackson
description: Jaafar Jackson, born 25 July 1996 in Los Angeles, California, is an American singer and actor, the son of Jermaine Jackson and the nephew of Michael Jackson. Raised inside one of popular music's most famous families, he began playing piano at age twelve and developed as a singer before releasing his debut single, "Got Me Singing," in 2019. In January 2023, after a worldwide casting search, Lionsgate announced that he would portray his uncle Michael in the biographical film Michael, directed by Antoine Fuqua and written by John Logan — his first acting role. The production cast him, in producer Graham King's account, because he personified his uncle's spirit and personality beyond any candidate found in the search. Michael premiered in Berlin on 10 April 2026 and was released in the United States on 24 April 2026, covering Michael Jackson's life from the Jackson 5 years through the Bad tour era. For the musical sequences Jaafar sang live over his uncle's recordings, blending his own voice with the original tracks. The role made a first-time actor the screen bearer of his own family's story.

name: Jaden Smith
description: Jaden Smith, born Jaden Christopher Syre Smith on 8 July 1998 in Malibu, California, is an American actor, rapper and singer, the son of Will Smith and Jada Pinkett Smith. He made his film debut at age eight opposite his father in The Pursuit of Happyness (2006), winning the MTV Movie Award for breakthrough performance, and starred in the remakes The Day the Earth Stood Still (2008) and The Karate Kid (2010), the latter alongside Jackie Chan. His feature on Justin Bieber's "Never Say Never" (2010), recorded for The Karate Kid, reached the Top 10 of the Billboard Hot 100 and was certified five-times platinum by the RIAA. He starred again with his father in After Earth (2013) and led the Netflix series The Get Down (2016). As a recording artist he released the studio albums Syre (2017), Erys (2019) and CTV3: Cool Tape Vol. 3 (2020), each entering the Top 40 of the Billboard 200, and he was nominated for the Grammy Award for Album of the Year as a featured artist on Bieber's Justice (2022). In September 2025 he was appointed Christian Louboutin's first men's creative director.

name: Jasmine Cephas Jones
description: Jasmine Cephas Jones, born 21 July 1989 in London, England, and raised in Midwood, Brooklyn, is an American actress and singer, the daughter of actor Ron Cephas Jones and jazz singer Kim Lesley. Trained at LaGuardia High School and Berklee College of Music, she graduated from the Neighborhood Playhouse School of the Theatre in 2011 and built early credits in independent film and television. In 2015 she originated the dual roles of Peggy Schuyler and Maria Reynolds in Hamilton, moving with the production from Off-Broadway to Broadway and remaining until December 2016; she won a Grammy Award as a principal soloist on the cast album. On screen she played Ashley in the film Blindspotting (2018), a role she reprised as star and producer of the Starz series of the same name (2021–2023). In 2020 she won the Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Actress in a Short Form Comedy or Drama Series for #FreeRayshawn, the first Black woman to win that category; her father won his own Emmy at the same ceremony, making them the first father-daughter duo to win Emmy Awards in the same year. Her debut album, Phoenix, arrived in 2024.

name: Journal of Blacks in Higher Education
aliases: The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education; JBHE
description: The Journal of Blacks in Higher Education (JBHE) is a publication founded in 1993 as a quarterly concerned with African Americans in academia and with racial equity in United States higher education. Its founder and longtime editor-in-chief was Theodore Cross, a civil rights advocate and businessman; Robert Bruce Slater served as managing editor and is the editor named in the journal's reference listings. The journal built its reputation on institution-by-institution statistical reporting on Black students and faculty, and scholars Rhonda Sharpe and William Darity have called it a key resource for publicly consumable statistical reports on the status of Blacks in higher education. Print publication ended with the spring issue in 2010, after Cross's death that February; the 1993–2010 issues are archived on JSTOR, and JBHE has continued publishing on its website and through a weekly bulletin.

name: Jalen Hurts
description: Jalen Alexander Hurts (born August 7, 1998, in Houston, Texas) is an American professional football quarterback for the Philadelphia Eagles of the National Football League. A coach's son, he was coached by his father Averion at Channelview High School in Texas, then played college football at Alabama from 2016 to 2018, where he was part of the 2017 national championship team, before finishing his college career at Oklahoma in 2019. Philadelphia drafted him in the second round of the 2020 NFL draft, 53rd overall, and he became the Eagles' starter late in his rookie season. In the 2022 season he led Philadelphia to Super Bowl LVII — the first Super Bowl to feature two Black starting quarterbacks, Hurts and Patrick Mahomes — and earned second-team All-Pro and Pro Bowl honors while finishing second in AP NFL Most Valuable Player voting. On February 9, 2025, he led the Eagles to a 40–22 victory over Kansas City in Super Bowl LIX and was voted the game's Most Valuable Player. Hurts remains Philadelphia's starting quarterback in the 2026 season, among the defining Black quarterbacks of his generation.

name: Julián Quiñones
description: Julián Quiñones, born Julián Andrés Quiñones Quiñones on 24 March 1997 in Magüí Payán, Nariño, Colombia, is an Afro-Colombian professional footballer who plays as a forward for Al-Qadsiah of the Saudi Pro League and, by naturalization, for the Mexico national team. Raised in Colombia's Pacific-coast Afro-Colombian heartland, he entered Tigres UANL's youth system in 2015 and built his name at Atlas, winning back-to-back Liga MX titles (Apertura 2021 and Clausura 2022), before a permanent Atlas move, a 2023 transfer to Club América that brought two further league titles, and a June 2024 move to Al-Qadsiah reported at the time as the most expensive sale by a Mexican club. Naturalized as a Mexican citizen in October 2023, he won the 2025 CONCACAF Gold Cup with Mexico and scored the opening goal of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, against South Africa on 11 June 2026. He finished the 2025–26 Saudi season as the league's Golden Boot winner.

name: Ja Morant
description: Ja Morant, born Temetrius Jamel Morant on 10 August 1999 in Dalzell, South Carolina, is an American professional basketball player for the Portland Trail Blazers. Lightly recruited out of Crestwood High School, he starred at Murray State, where as a sophomore he became the first player since assists became an official statistic to average 20 points and 10 assists in a season, won the Bob Cousy Award and was a consensus first-team All-American. Memphis drafted him second overall in 2019; he was Rookie of the Year in 2020, Most Improved Player and an All-NBA selection in 2022, and a two-time All-Star who led the Grizzlies to consecutive No. 2 seeds. Injuries and league suspensions — eight games in March 2023 and 25 games to open 2023-24, both over firearm incidents on social media — limited him to 79 games across his final three Memphis seasons. On 29 June 2026 Memphis traded him to Portland for Jerami Grant and Kris Murray, ending a seven-season tenure in which he averaged 22.4 points and 7.4 assists.

name: Jayson Tatum
description: Jayson Tatum, born Jayson Christopher Tatum on 3 March 1998 in St. Louis, Missouri, is an American professional basketball player for the Boston Celtics. The Gatorade National Player of the Year at Chaminade College Preparatory School, he played one season at Duke before Boston selected him third overall in the 2017 NBA draft. A six-time All-Star and four-time All-NBA First Team selection, he was the Eastern Conference finals MVP in 2022 and led Boston to the 2024 NBA championship, the franchise's first title since 2008. He also won Olympic gold medals with the United States in Tokyo in 2021 and Paris in 2024. In May 2025 he ruptured his Achilles tendon; he returned in March 2026 and averaged 21.7 points across Boston's final regular-season games before knee stiffness held him out of the Celtics' final playoff game. By October 2026 he was healthy, leading a reworked Boston roster into his tenth season after the trade of Jaylen Brown.

name: Jared McCain
description: Jared McCain, born Jared Dane McCain on 20 February 2004 in Sacramento, California, is an American shooting guard for the Oklahoma City Thunder. His father, Lance McCain, is African-American, and McCain — a consensus five-star recruit at Centennial High School in Corona, twice California's Gatorade Player of the Year and the state's Mr. Basketball in 2023 — has also acknowledged a partial Filipino heritage. At Duke he made the ACC All-Rookie team in his single season, and Philadelphia selected him 16th overall in the 2024 NBA draft. As a rookie he led all rookies in scoring at 15.3 points per game and was named Eastern Conference Rookie of the Month for October-November 2024 before a December 2024 injury ended his season on 13 December. After a limited role in Philadelphia in 2025-26, he was traded to Oklahoma City at the February 2026 deadline and averaged 10.4 points in 30 regular-season games for the Thunder, then 12.5 points across eleven games in the Lakers and Spurs playoff series, starting two Western Conference Finals games. name: Jason Taylor
description: Jason Taylor, born Jason Paul Taylor on 1 September 1974 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, is a retired American football defensive end whose fifteen-season career was anchored by the Miami Dolphins. A lightly recruited player who starred at the University of Akron, where he set a school record with 21 career sacks, he was selected by Miami in the third round, 73rd overall, of the 1997 NFL Draft and became a starter as a rookie. He anchored Miami's defense for more than a decade, led the NFL with 18.5 sacks in 2002, and in 2006 was named NFL Defensive Player of the Year. After single seasons with Washington in 2008 and the New York Jets in 2010, each followed by a return to Miami, he retired after the 2011 season with 139.5 career sacks. He was elected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame in 2017, in his first year of eligibility, and has coached at the University of Miami since 2022, serving as the Hurricanes' defensive ends and rush coach from 2023 into the 2026 season.

description: Justin Jefferson, born Justin Jamal Jefferson on 16 June 1999 in St. Rose, Louisiana, is an American football wide receiver for the Minnesota Vikings. He played at Destrehan High School and at LSU, where he helped the Tigers win the College Football Playoff national championship for the 2019 season. Minnesota selected him 22nd overall in the 2020 NFL Draft, and he answered with 1,400 receiving yards as a rookie. He has exceeded 1,000 receiving yards in every season of his career, including seasons shortened by injury. His 2022 season set the standard: he led the NFL with 128 receptions and 1,809 receiving yards and was named the Associated Press NFL Offensive Player of the Year. Through the first five weeks of the 2026 season he remained Minnesota's No. 1 receiver, recording 19 receptions for 258 yards and three touchdowns across four games played, and his career totals stood at 598 receptions for 8,738 yards and 45 receiving touchdowns in 98 games, all with the Vikings.

name: Jeremiah Smith
description: Jeremiah Smith, born Jeremiah Javon Smith on 29 November 2005 in Miami Gardens, Florida, is an American college football wide receiver for the Ohio State Buckeyes. He attended Chaminade-Madonna Prep in Hollywood, Florida, and arrived at Ohio State as one of the most heralded recruits in the country. As a true freshman in 2024 he caught 76 passes for 1,315 yards and 15 touchdowns, breaking FBS freshman receiving records, and helped Ohio State win the College Football Playoff national championship. As a sophomore in 2025 he added 87 receptions for 1,243 yards and 12 touchdowns and was named a unanimous All-American. By October of his junior season in 2026 he had broken all three of Ohio State's major career receiving records — receptions, receiving yards, and touchdown receptions — passing marks held by Emeka Egbuka, Michael Jenkins, and Chris Olave, and his career totals stood at 211 receptions for 3,474 yards and 38 touchdowns. name: Jaxon Smith-Njigba
description: Jaxon Smith-Njigba, born 14 February 2002 in Nacogdoches, Texas, is an American football wide receiver for the Seattle Seahawks. He is of Sierra Leonean descent through his father: his paternal grandparents came from Sierra Leone, and as a high-school player he added "Njigba" — his grandfather's original surname, set aside for "Smith" on immigrating to the United States in the 1970s — to his own name to honor him. Raised in Rockwall, Texas, he starred at Ohio State, where his 347 receiving yards against Utah in the Rose Bowl on 1 January 2022 set the bowl's record. Seattle selected him 20th overall in the 2023 NFL Draft. In 2025 he led the NFL with 1,793 receiving yards on 119 receptions, was named NFL Offensive Player of the Year, and helped Seattle win Super Bowl LX over New England in February 2026. That spring the Seahawks signed him to a four-year, $168.6 million extension, reported as the richest contract ever given to a wide receiver. He remains Seattle's No. 1 receiver in the 2026 season.

name: Joe Louis
aliases: Joseph Louis Barrow; The Brown Bomber
description: Joe Louis (born Joseph Louis Barrow, May 13, 1914, LaFayette, Alabama; died April 12, 1981, Paradise, Nevada) was the world heavyweight boxing champion from 1937 to 1949 and the most consequential Black athlete of his century. Raised in Detroit, he won the 1934 national AAU light-heavyweight title and took the heavyweight crown from James J. Braddock on June 22, 1937, at Chicago's Comiskey Park, knocking Braddock out in the eighth round. Louis had lost to Germany's Max Schmeling in 1936; their rematch on June 22, 1938, before 70,043 at Yankee Stadium, ended in two minutes and four seconds of the first round and was read worldwide as democracy's answer to Nazi racial doctrine. Louis defended the title 25 times, a division record, and his reign made him a unifying national hero and the standard against which Black athletic greatness was measured for a generation.

name: James R. Grossman
description: James R. Grossman is the historian whose Land of Hope: Chicago, Black Southerners, and the Great Migration (1989) set the scholarly frame for Chicago's Great Migration history — the book is already in this graph at CTL-E-5850, and this record completes its authorship. Grossman earned his bachelor's degree at Cornell and his doctorate at the University of California, Berkeley, taught at the University of Chicago and UC San Diego, and served as vice president for research and education at the Newberry Library in Chicago. His second book, A Chance to Make Good: African Americans 1900–1929, appeared in 1997, and he was a project director and co-editor of the Encyclopedia of Chicago. From 2010 to 2025 he served as executive director of the American Historical Association. In 2025 the Society of American Historians awarded him its Tony Horwitz Prize, honoring his leadership of the historical profession.

name: Jesse Owens
description: Jesse Owens (James Cleveland Owens, born September 12, 1913, Oakville, Alabama; died March 31, 1980, Tucson, Arizona, of lung cancer, aged 66) was the track athlete whose four gold medals at the 1936 Berlin Olympics became the century's most famous athletic refutation of a racial doctrine. His family moved to Cleveland in 1922; at East Technical High School he tied the national 100-yard record of 9.4 seconds as a senior. At Ohio State — in an era without athletic scholarships, working part-time jobs — he produced sport's most famous afternoon: on May 25, 1935, at Ann Arbor, he set three world records and tied a fourth in about forty-five minutes, across the 100-yard dash, the long jump, the 220-yard dash, and the 220-yard low hurdles. In Berlin in August 1936 he won the 100 meters, the 200 meters, the long jump, and the 4×100-meter relay, the relay in a world-record 39.8 seconds. He came home to segregation and financial hardship. The nation honored him late: the Presidential Medal of Freedom in 1976 and a posthumous Congressional Gold Medal in 1990.

name: Jayden Daniels
description: Jayden Daniels, born 18 December 2000 in Fontana, California, is an American professional football quarterback for the Washington Commanders. He began his college career at Arizona State, starting for three seasons, then transferred to LSU, where his second season, in 2023, became one of the most productive in college football history. At LSU he threw for 3,812 yards and 40 touchdowns against four interceptions and ran for 1,134 yards and ten more scores, leading the nation in total offense and winning the Heisman Trophy, the Davey O'Brien Award and AP Player of the Year. Washington drafted him second overall in 2024. As a rookie he set several rookie records, won NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year, made the Pro Bowl and led Washington to its first NFC Championship Game appearance since the 1991 season. Injuries interrupted his 2025 campaign and the start of 2026, including a dislocated left elbow in Week 2, but he returned to start in October 2026, in his third NFL season.

name: Ja'Marr Chase
description: Ja'Marr Chase, born Ja'Marr Anthony Chase on 1 March 2000 in Harvey, Louisiana, is an American professional football wide receiver for the Cincinnati Bengals. At LSU he was Joe Burrow's leading target on the 2019 national-championship team, winning the Fred Biletnikoff Award as the nation's top receiver that season before opting out of 2020. Cincinnati drafted him fifth overall in 2021, reuniting him with Burrow. He set the rookie single-game receiving record, won NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year and reached Super Bowl LVI in his first season. After Pro Bowl seasons that established him among the league's elite, in 2024 he won the receiving triple crown — leading the NFL in receptions, receiving yards and receiving touchdowns — only the fifth player in the Super Bowl era to do so. He followed it with another First-team All-Pro season in 2025 and remained Cincinnati's No. 1 receiver in October 2026, scoring in the Bengals' Week 5 win at Miami.

name: Jahmyr Gibbs
description: Jahmyr Gibbs, born 20 March 2002 in Dalton, Georgia, is an American professional football running back for the Detroit Lions. A dual-threat back at Georgia Tech, he transferred to Alabama for 2022, averaging 6.1 yards per carry and catching 44 passes in his single season with the Crimson Tide. Detroit selected him 12th overall in the 2023 NFL draft, a pick widely questioned at the time and quickly vindicated. Paired first with David Montgomery in Detroit's backfield, Gibbs made the Pro Bowl in each of his first three seasons. In 2024 he set a Detroit franchise record with 20 total touchdowns, leading the league, and scored four times in the Week 18 game that clinched the NFC's top seed. In October 2026 he was named NFC Offensive Player of the Week after a 207-yard scrimmage game at Arizona, in which he passed Barry Sanders for the most touchdowns scored before age 25 in NFL history.

name: José Ramírez
description: José Ramírez, born 17 September 1992 in Baní, Dominican Republic, is a switch-hitting third baseman who has spent his entire major league career with Cleveland. Signed as an amateur free agent at 17, he debuted on 1 September 2013 and broke through in 2016, helping Cleveland reach that year's World Series. He became the franchise's defining player: a six-time Silver Slugger winner who has finished in the top five of American League MVP voting six times and rewritten the club record book, leading the franchise in extra-base hits. Rather than test free agency, Ramírez signed successive extensions to stay in Cleveland, most recently a seven-year, $175 million deal in January 2026, declaring himself “50% Dominican, 50% Clevelander.” In October 2026 he was still Cleveland's engine, producing in the club's postseason series. name: Juan Soto
aliases: Juan José Soto Pacheco; Childish Bambino
description: Juan Soto, born 25 October 1998 in Santo Domingo, Dominican Republic, is the New York Mets' left fielder and one of the most disciplined hitters in baseball history. He debuted with Washington in 2018 at 19 and was a cornerstone of the Nationals' 2019 World Series championship. After trades to San Diego (2022) and the New York Yankees (2024), he signed a 15-year, $765 million contract with the Mets in December 2024 — the largest in North American sports. His first two Mets seasons ended without a playoff berth; in 2026, limited to 108 games by two calf-strain injured-list stints, he hit .275 with a .908 OPS and a team-leading 27 home runs, and publicly took responsibility for the club's failure, telling the New York Post in September 2026 that he had to be better. CTL stages him as an Afro-Dominican ballplayer; individual descent documentation is named as a gap below.

name: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
description: Jazz Chisholm Jr., born Jasrado Chisholm Jr. on 1 February 1998 in Nassau, Bahamas, is a Black Bahamian infielder for the New York Yankees and the most accomplished Bahamian player in major league history. Taught to hit at age two by his grandmother Patricia Coakley, a shortstop for the Bahamian national softball team, he moved to Kansas at twelve for high school, signed with the Arizona Diamondbacks as an international free agent in 2015, and debuted for the Miami Marlins on 1 September 2020. In 2022 he became the first Bahamian-born player selected to an MLB All-Star team, and he was the cover athlete for MLB The Show 23. Traded to the Yankees in July 2024, he produced his best season in 2025 with 31 home runs, 80 RBIs and 31 stolen bases, earning a second All-Star selection and a Silver Slugger Award. In 2026 he hit 19 home runs with 41 stolen bases in 137 games, and he became a free agent after the Yankees' Division Series loss in October 2026.

name: Joe Frazier
description: Joe Frazier (born Joseph William Frazier on 12 January 1944 in Beaufort, South Carolina; died 7 November 2011 in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania) was an American heavyweight boxer, Olympic champion and undisputed world heavyweight champion whose relentless pressure style and powerful left hook defined boxing's great heavyweight era. He reached the 1964 Tokyo Olympics as a replacement for the injured Buster Mathis, who had beaten him in the trials, and won heavyweight gold. He turned professional in August 1965, and on 16 February 1970 knocked out Jimmy Ellis in five rounds to become undisputed champion. On 8 March 1971 he defeated Muhammad Ali by unanimous decision in the Fight of the Century at Madison Square Garden, handing Ali the first loss of his career and flooring him in the final round. He lost the title to George Foreman in January 1973, lost a rematch with Ali in 1974, and lost their brutal third meeting, the Thrilla in Manila, in October 1975. He retired in 1976, made a one-fight comeback in 1981, and entered the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1990. Tribute record: he died of liver cancer, aged 67.

name: Jesmyn Ward
description: Jesmyn Ward is a Mississippi novelist, memoirist, and professor of creative writing at Tulane University whose fiction is rooted in the Black communities of the Mississippi Gulf Coast, including her hometown of DeLisle. She received her MFA from the University of Michigan, held a Stegner Fellowship at Stanford from 2008 to 2010, and served as Grisham Writer in Residence at the University of Mississippi. Her novel Salvage the Bones, set around Hurricane Katrina, won the National Book Award for Fiction in 2011, and Sing, Unburied, Sing won the same award in 2017, making her a two-time winner. Her memoir Men We Reaped, mourning five young Black men lost in her community, was a finalist for the National Book Critics Circle Award. She edited the anthology The Fire This Time, received a MacArthur Fellowship in 2017, and later published the novel Let Us Descend. Her work joins lyrical, formally inventive prose to an unsparing record of poverty, kinship, grief, and endurance in the rural Black South.

name: Jackie Wilson
aliases: Jack Leroy Wilson Jr.; Mr. Excitement
description: Jack Leroy Wilson Jr. (June 9, 1934 – January 21, 1984), born in Detroit's Highland Park enclave, was a singer whose athletic, operatic performances helped carry rhythm and blues into soul. He first gained fame as lead singer of Billy Ward and His Dominoes, replacing Clyde McPhatter, and went solo in 1957. Nicknamed 'Mr. Excitement,' he scored more than fifty chart singles across R&B, pop, soul, and doo-wop, including 'Reet Petite,' 'Lonely Teardrops,' 'Baby Workout,' and '(Your Love Keeps Lifting Me) Higher and Higher,' several early hits co-written by a young Berry Gordy Jr. His spins, splits, and vocal range made him a formative influence on Elvis Presley, James Brown, and Michael Jackson. In September 1975 he suffered a heart attack on stage during a benefit performance and remained in a minimally conscious state until his death in 1984 at age forty-nine. He was inducted into the Rock and Roll Hall of Fame in 1987, and two of his recordings entered the Grammy Hall of Fame in 1999.

name: Josh Gibson
aliases: Joshua Gibson; the Black Babe Ruth
description: Josh Gibson, born December 21, 1911, in Buena Vista, Georgia, and raised in Pittsburgh from 1923, was the catcher regarded as the greatest power hitter of the Negro leagues. His professional start was accidental: on July 25, 1930, sitting in the stands, he was called in to replace the Homestead Grays' injured catcher, and he stayed. Gibson played for the Grays in 1930-1931, starred for the Pittsburgh Crawfords from 1932 to 1936, and returned to the Grays from 1937 to 1939 and 1942 to 1946, with seasons in the Dominican and Mexican leagues between. A 6-foot-1 catcher with a powerful arm and quick release, he hit for average and immense distance, winning consecutive batting Triple Crowns, a feat no batter has matched since. Segregation's unwritten agreement barred him from the American and National Leagues for his entire career. He died in Pittsburgh on January 20, 1947, months before Jackie Robinson's major-league debut, and in 1972 became the second Negro league player elected to the National Baseball Hall of Fame, after Satchel Paige.

name: Jordan Chiles
description: Jordan Chiles, born 15 April 2001 in Tualatin, Oregon, is an American artistic gymnast. Her father is Black and her mother is Latina, and she was named after basketball player Michael Jordan. A member of the United States national team for a USA Gymnastics-record 11 years, she won team silver at the Tokyo 2020 Olympics and team gold at Paris 2024, and at the 2022 World Championships took team gold and silver on vault and floor exercise. In 2019 she moved to Spring, Texas, to train alongside Simone Biles at the World Champions Centre. At UCLA (2021–26) she became a 23-time All-American, a seven-time conference champion and a 19-time perfect-10 scorer, won NCAA titles on uneven bars (2023, 2025) and floor exercise (2026), and as a senior in 2026 won the AAI Award as the nation's top senior gymnast. She is finishing a degree in African American Studies, authored the New York Times best-seller I'm That Girl, and was a TIME Woman of the Year in 2025. In 2026 she joined UCLA's 2027 staff as a student coach and announced an elite return aimed at Los Angeles 2028.

name: Jann Mardenborough
description: Jann Alexander Mardenborough, born 9 September 1991 in Darlington, England, and raised in Cardiff, Wales, is a British professional racing driver who reached the sport without a karting background. The son of former professional footballer Steve Mardenborough, he was a devoted player of the Gran Turismo video games when, in 2011, he won Nissan's GT Academy competition against some 90,000 entrants, becoming its third and youngest winner and earning a professional contract. He finished third in class on his Le Mans debut in 2013, won races in British GT and the GP3 Series, raced Nissan's LMP1 car in the 2015 World Endurance Championship, and then built a second career in Japan, winning in Super GT's GT300 class, finishing runner-up in Japanese Formula 3 in 2016 and taking a Super Formula pole position in 2017. The 2023 film Gran Turismo dramatized his story, with Mardenborough serving as co-producer, consultant and his own stunt driver. In 2025 he was racing a Ford Mustang GT3 for HRT Ford Performance in the GT World Challenge Europe Endurance Cup, one of very few Black drivers at the international level of endurance racing.
